common_name: Krelagei Crinum Lily (Deep Rosy-Red Hardy Swamp Lily)

planting.note: Set bulbs with the neck at or just below soil level in rich, well-drained garden soil in full sun to light shade; this old Dutch-raised selection tolerates winter cold better than most crinums and rarely needs lifting.

directions: A long-cultivated selection of the classic hardy hybrid Crinum x powellii, 'Krelagei' bears tall scapes of deep rosy-red, trumpet-shaped flowers above broad, strap-like foliage in mid to late summer. It is among the cold-hardiest of the large-flowered crinums, surviving winters well north of where most tropical species persist, which has kept it in Southern dooryard gardens for generations alongside the paler 'Album' and 'Roseum' forms. Clumps bulk up steadily and are best left undisturbed for years, since flowering improves as the planting matures and becomes congested. Division in early spring is only needed to propagate new plants or rejuvenate an overcrowded bed.
sources: Scott Ogden's Garden Bulbs for the South

planting.note: Plant bulbs shallowly in constantly moist, acidic, sandy soil in partial shade; this diminutive spiderlily comes from seepage slopes and bog margins of the Florida Panhandle and needs steady moisture year-round to thrive.

directions: One of the smallest members of its genus, dwarf spiderlily grows naturally in wet, acidic seepage bogs and pitcher-plant savannas of the Florida Panhandle, forming tight clumps of narrow leaves well under a foot tall. Its white, spidery flowers appear in summer and are proportionally smaller than those of the larger Gulf Coast spiderlilies but share the same fragrant, long-tepaled form. Because it comes from permanently saturated, mineral-poor seeps, it performs best in a boggy container, rain garden, or constructed wetland rather than an ordinary border. It is a good companion for other pitcher-plant-bog natives that share its demand for constant moisture and acidic, sandy substrate.
sources: Scott Ogden's Garden Bulbs for the South

planting.note: Plant bulbs in moist, sandy to peaty, acidic soil along a pond edge or rain garden in partial shade to full sun; this rare Florida Panhandle native is restricted in the wild to wet flatwoods and seepage areas.

directions: Named for botanist Robert K. Godfrey, this spiderlily is a narrow Florida Panhandle endemic found in wet pine flatwoods and seasonally flooded savannas, where it produces fragrant white flowers with the characteristic funnel-shaped staminal cup in late spring and summer. Its range is small enough that the species is considered rare in the wild, making garden cultivation a worthwhile way to keep it in circulation among bulb enthusiasts. In cultivation it wants the same constantly moist, acidic conditions as its wild habitat, doing best at a pond margin or in a boggy raised bed rather than average garden soil. Give it space to form a slowly spreading clump and avoid letting the planting site dry out during summer.
sources: Scott Ogden's Garden Bulbs for the South

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in moist, humus-rich soil along streambanks, ditch margins, or pond edges in partial shade to full sun, mimicking the low wet woods of the western Gulf Coast where it grows wild.

directions: Shortleaf spiderlily is a Gulf Coast native found in low, periodically flooded woods and roadside ditches from Louisiana into Texas, distinguished from its larger relatives by comparatively broad, thick leaves and clustered white, evening-fragrant flowers in late spring. Like other wetland Hymenocallis, it draws sphinx moths after dusk and is best appreciated from a path or patio where the fragrance can be enjoyed on summer evenings. The species tolerates both standing water during wet seasons and drier spells once established, making it adaptable to rain gardens and bioswales as well as consistently damp beds. Clumps increase gradually by offset bulbs and need little attention beyond ensuring they are never allowed to dry out for extended periods.
sources: Scott Ogden's Garden Bulbs for the South

common_name: Fairy Moon Rain Lily (Pastel Pink Hybrid Rain Lily)

planting.note: Plant small bulbs 2-3 inches deep in well-drained garden soil in full sun to light shade; like other rain lilies, this hybrid flushes into bloom within days of a good warm-season rain.

directions: A popular pass-along hybrid among Southern rain lily collectors, 'Fairy Moon' produces unusually large, soft pink-blushed flowers that fade toward a pale, almost luminous center, giving the cultivar its evocative name. Like other Zephyranthes, it blooms in flushes tied to rainfall, sending up a crop of flowers within a few days of a good soaking after dry weather, from late spring through fall. The grassy foliage stays low and tidy between bloom cycles, making it useful as an edging or rock garden bulb that earns its space with repeated surprise color. Established clumps multiply by offset bulbs and can be divided every few years in early spring to spread the planting or share with other gardeners.
sources: Scott Ogden's Garden Bulbs for the South

common_name: Big Dude Rain Lily (Large-Flowered Pink Hybrid Rain Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun; this vigorous hybrid produces notably larger flowers than most rain lilies and benefits from slightly richer soil to support the bigger blooms.

directions: True to its name, 'Big Dude' is a rain lily hybrid selected for flowers considerably larger than the species norm, opening in a rich pink that deepens toward the throat after a warm-season rain. It shares the familiar rain lily habit of staying inconspicuous between bloom flushes, then surprising the gardener with a crop of oversized, upward-facing flowers within a few days of rainfall from late spring into fall. The strap-like foliage is sturdier than that of the smaller species to support the larger blooms, and clumps bulk up steadily when left undisturbed. It is a favorite among Southern bulb collectors for front-of-border plantings where its size makes a stronger show than typical rain lilies.
sources: Scott Ogden's Garden Bulbs for the South

planting.note: Plant small bulbs 2 inches deep in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; this Chihuahuan Desert native wants far less summer water than Gulf Coast rain lilies and resents heavy, wet clay.

directions: Plains zephyr lily is a small, drought-tolerant rain lily native to limestone and caliche soils of the Trans-Pecos and southern Plains, bearing slender, grass-like leaves and bright yellow flowers often brushed with copper or bronze on the outer petal surface. Like its Gulf Coast cousins it blooms in response to rain following a dry spell, but it is adapted to far leaner, rockier conditions and suffers in rich, constantly moist border soil. It is best grown in a rock garden, gravel bed, or raised planting where drainage is sharp, paired with other dryland bulbs rather than the wetland-loving Zephyranthes and Hymenocallis of the coastal plain. Clumps are slow to bulk up but persist for decades once settled into a well-drained site.
sources: Scott Ogden's Garden Bulbs for the South

planting.note: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun; set out in spring and expect flushes of bloom after warm-season rains through summer and fall.

directions: Habranthus concolor bears clear golden-yellow flowers, uniformly colored throughout as the species name suggests, carried singly on slender stems in the slightly tilted, funnel-shaped form typical of the genus. Native to Mexico, it has long circulated among Southern bulb gardeners as a reliable warm-season rain lily that flushes into bloom days after a good soaking rain, much like the more commonly grown Habranthus robustus and tubispathus. Its fine, grassy foliage stays inconspicuous between bloom cycles, letting it tuck into a sunny border or rock garden without drawing attention until a rain event triggers a fresh crop of flowers. Established plantings slowly increase by offset bulbs and self-sown seedlings in favorable years.
sources: Scott Ogden's Garden Bulbs for the South

planting.note: Plant bulbs in late summer with the neck near the soil surface in well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade; leave established clumps undisturbed, since Lycoris bloom best when left to mature for several years.

directions: A naturally occurring Japanese hybrid between two spider lily species, peppermint spiderlily opens pale pink flowers brushed with a deeper rose stripe down the center of each petal, giving an effect reminiscent of its candy-striped namesake. Like Lycoris radiata it follows the classic leafless 'surprise lily' cycle, pushing up bare flower stalks in late summer before strap-like foliage emerges afterward and persists through winter. Its coloring sets it apart from the familiar red hurricane lily and the pale pink naked ladies common in Southern gardens, offering collectors a subtler bicolor option for the same fall display. Grow it as part of a Lycoris collection in partial shade beneath deciduous trees where its summer dormancy goes unnoticed under the leaf canopy.
sources: Scott Ogden's Garden Bulbs for the South

planting.note: Plant bulbs in late summer with the neck near the soil surface in well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; this natural hybrid between golden and red spider lilies is undemanding once established.

directions: Straw spiderlily is a natural Japanese hybrid between the golden spider lily, Lycoris aurea, and the familiar red hurricane lily, Lycoris radiata, producing pale creamy-yellow flowers with a faint warm blush that splits the difference between its two parents. It follows the same dramatic leafless flowering cycle shared by its parents, sending up bare stalks topped with umbels of spidery flowers in late summer before the strap-like leaves emerge and overwinter as a low groundcover. The soft straw coloring gives fall bulb plantings a gentler note among the more common vivid reds and pinks, and it combines well with both of its parent species in a mixed Lycoris bed. As with other members of the genus, undisturbed clumps left for several years produce the fullest flowering display.
sources: Scott Ogden's Garden Bulbs for the South

planting.note: Plant bulbs in late summer with the neck near the soil surface in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; this Korean species is cold-hardier than many tender Lycoris and suits a woodland edge planting.

directions: Native to Jeju Island off the southern coast of Korea, this species bears soft lavender-pink flowers in late summer, following the same leafless surprise-lily habit as its better-known relatives, with strap-shaped foliage emerging after bloom and persisting through the cooler months. Specialty bulb growers prize it for its cold hardiness relative to more tender Lycoris species and for a flower color intermediate between the pink of naked ladies and the lavender tones seen in some Lycoris sprengeri forms. It remains relatively uncommon in Southern gardens compared to the ubiquitous red hurricane lily, making it a worthwhile addition for collectors assembling a broader Lycoris collection. Give it humus-rich, well-drained soil at a woodland edge and leave clumps undisturbed to build toward their best flowering.
